newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis mourn loss of life in market "inferno".
newsitem.headline: Israelis mourn loss of life in market "inferno".

text.p: The front pages of Israeli newspapers on Thursday reflected the depth of sorrow and fury over the suicide bombings that blew apart the main Jewish market in Jerusalem.
Israel mourned the deaths of 13 people on Wednesday at the hands of two Moslem suicide bombers. More than 80 people remained in hospital.
"Inferno in the market," screamed the headline across the country's biggest daily Yedioth Ahronoth.
It and the rival Maariv published huge photos of bloodied and blackened men, women and children wounded by the blasts.
"The terrorism is back," read the headline over a front-page commentary.

The Mahane Yehuda market itself opened for business, its stall owners vowing not to be hampered by the attack. Israeli radio stations broadcast the times and locations for the first funerals while playing sombre songs.
City workers spent the night removing debris and cleaning the street market, which was packed with shoppers early on Thursday.
Uri Mizrahi, owner of a delicatessen, told Israeli army radio: "I arrived at 5:30. I opened the business as usual. Nothing can break us."

The Victims of Arab Terror group and other right-wing movements planned a protest in Jerusalem to urge going ahead with construction of a Jewish settler enclave in Arab East Jerusalem which the government had stopped following Palestinian anger.

The liberal newspaper Haaretz wrote in an editorial: "No political dispute or religious disagreement justifies or excuses the murder...and the wounding of dozens, including women and children, in the Mahane Yehuda market in Jerusalem.
"It is clear that no policy, or regime, immunises the citizens of Israel from Palestinian suicide attackers sent to sow murder and terror in the population centres of Israel."
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, elected 14 months ago, had only in recent days credited his tough policy with having curbed Arab attacks on Israelis despite a crisis in Middle East peacemaking.

Maariv diplomatic commentator Chemi Shalev wrote that the attack would divert the attention of the United States -- the main Middle East peace broker -- from Israeli settlement construction in Arab East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The settlement issue had already brought peace talks with the Palestinians to a standstill.
Left-wing Israeli author David Grossman wrote in a Maariv front-page commentary that Washington must get more involved to save Israelis and Palestinians from themselves.

"It seems to me the latest blast requires us to recognise reality for what it is: Israel and the Palestinians alone are incapable any longer of reaching an agreement on their own that will ensure true peace," Grossman wrote.

"They are captives to their history and psychology, and have lost the ability to escape it. If anyone in the world still cares what is happening here, it is better that he do something to force the leaders of the sides to begin talking seriously.

"The American style of 'letting the sides ripen on their own' has proven to be ineffective when speaking of two peoples with our suicidal tendencies. Now what's essential is decisive outside pressure on the two sides, and mainly on Israel which holds most of the cards in its hands."
